stem:
Monique is a 16-year-old girl with previously well-controlled persistent asthma. Over the last few months she has had more symptoms than usual, with a fall in her lung function confirmed on testing today. When questioned directly, Monique admits that she forgot to take her fluticasone (Flixotide) 3–4 days last week. She carries her salbutamol (Ventolin) in her bag and has used that 4 times in the last week.

What is the best approach to improve Monique’s asthma management?

options.text: Tell her that inhalers should not be kept in her bag
Lecture her about taking responsibility for her own health
Tell her her parents must remind her to take her inhaler
Discuss strategies that Monique thinks will help to improve her asthma management
Ask her boyfriend to help remind her to take her inhaler

explanation: For an adolescent with poor asthma control related to missed preventer doses, the best approach is collaborative self-management: explore barriers, involve Monique in choosing practical strategies, and support adherence in a way that fits her routine. This is more effective than blaming, lecturing, or defaulting to parent/partner reminders.

citations.title: Practice Quiz: Asthma Management: Medications and Devices - Part B

rationale: Adolescent asthma management should be collaborative and centred on the young person’s perspective, aiming to identify barriers and agree on practical adherence strategies.

optionExplanations.A: Where the inhaler is kept is not the main issue; the problem is adherence to the preventer regimen.
optionExplanations.B: A lecturing approach is unlikely to improve adherence and may reduce engagement.
optionExplanations.C: Parents can support, but adolescents should be engaged in shared decision-making and self-management.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: patient-centred discussion of strategies she thinks will work is the best way to improve adherence.
optionExplanations.E: A boyfriend may be supportive, but this is not the best or most appropriate primary strategy.
